narratives.common: Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Austin, Texas factory, with the end expected around mid-2027, after years of weak sales. The space is to be used for the Cybercab robotaxi, and Musk's earlier claim that the Cybertruck would be Tesla's 'best product ever' is cited in several reports.

groups.distinct: Posts are mostly mocking and personal rather than reportive. They use insults such as 'WankPanzer', 'NaziTruck' and 'IncelCamino', and express schadenfreude about owners losing access to parts. A few share articles (TechCrunch, Curbed, Kotaku) and one mentions a '$92K last call' and a robotaxi with emergency controls as 'polite requests to the software'.

Commenters barely cover the announcement itself and instead debate the truck's merits. Topics include its roughly $82k price, its use as emergency home power, efficiency figures (2 mi/kWh against 3.8 for the Model Y), and towing range. Others call it a symbol of the Trump era or tie it to one political worldview, and one defends it as worth buying for Tesla's autonomous driving.

Coverage is mostly straightforward headlines focused on the Austin Gigafactory and the production timeline. Some add that the truck's 'allure' escaped most buyers, and MotorTrend calls it a 'slow-selling pickup'.

outlet_notes: The New York Times: center-left (AI estimate)
groups.distinct: These outlets lean toward verdicts on failure and cause. Defector calls it 'A Total Failure', NPR names 'insufficient demand' as the 'cause of death', and NBC says sales were poor 'in few markets'. The Times frames it as a refocus on the Cybercab.

Adds explainer and market angles, such as USA Today's 'what comes next' and Fortune's contrast with Musk's 'best product ever' claim. Ars Technica calls it an 'angular metallic flop'. Barron's item is about a broad Nasdaq sell-off hitting SpaceX and Tesla shares, not the Cybertruck.

Frames the story through Musk's quote, with the WSJ saying the Cybertruck is 'being scrapped'. Fox Business and Forbes stress making room for the Cybercab. The Investor's Business Daily item is about a SpaceX land deal and a Tesla merger in an election context, with no Cybertruck mention in the headline.
Adds the original ambition, citing '250,000-unit' hopes against the wind-down. Livemint asks 'what went wrong', while others stress weak sales and the Cybercab taking 'centre stage'.
Focuses on markets and uncertainty. One headline says Tesla stock rose 3%, and another says the model's future is left 'unclear'. Dezeen puts 'winding down' in quotation marks.

narrative:
Coverage of Tesla's Cybertruck wind-down splits into five framings, though only 54 of 160 items (34%) carried a framing. The agreement score (kappa 0.41) is flagged "unreliable," so the shares below are rough.

The largest framing, at 37% of framed items, is the neutral announcement, which reports Musk's statement and the Texas/2027 timing. In the sample, CBS News, The Washington Post, CNN, Bloomberg, NDTV, Euronews, The Telegraph and The Times fit this framing. Obituary and skeptical commentary follows at 24%, with Axios and Fortune, plus several Mastodon users using "RIP"-style language. Commercial flop (19%) appears in NBC News, Futurism's feed and several Hacker News commenters, who cite weak sales and product fit. The strategic pivot to Cybercab and AI (19%) appears in The Guardian, Financial Times and The New York Times. Quality and recall troubles is marginal (2%), with only Reuters in the sample.

No outlet or account carries a lean label; all are still "building." Each has a single item, so the placements are tentative and based on headlines and snippets. Sample sizes are small.

narratives.common: Democrats won control of the U.S. House in the 2026 midterms, flipping more than 40 seats, and coverage describes a broad "blue wave" and Republican losses. Several outlets report a razor-thin Mississippi Senate race still undecided and a post-election shake-up at the White House. Attention has also turned to what a Democratic Congress will do and to how Democrats will organize internally.

groups.distinct: Posts are opinionated and personal. They quote Hakeem Jeffries' leadership being contested, attack JD Vance and "tech fascists", and cite Thomas Massie's plan to force an impeachment vote on Pete Hegseth. They also discuss Elon Musk's near-$500 million spending and the AI-stock dip. One post warns that hearings without resignations would not be accountability.

Mostly topical explainer and advisory headlines from law firms, consultancies and universities, covering what the results mean for business, philanthropy and forecasting, and election-day interference threats. Pillsbury's headline says Trump "keeps the veto". Yahoo adds that Stephen Miller was named chief of staff and that Alaska and Mississippi were undecided.

groups.distinct: Frames results through market and ideological analysis: the Financial Times reports global stocks tumbling in an "AI rout", The Economist credits moderate Democrats for the wave, and Chatham House and ODI link the result to populism and 2028.

Reports that Rubio resignation rumours swirled amid a Republican "blame game". LSE Blogs argues the result may end Trumpism while "MAGA is here to stay", and Sky says Trump replaced his chief of staff.

Largely sidesteps the national scoreboard in favor of lighter or human-interest and culture-war angles: voter anger in suburban Bethesda, the "Arc De Trump", the Pope voting, and a claim about the Ilhan Omar investigation dying "on the vine" under Obama.

narrative:
Coverage of the 2026 US midterms splits into five framings, with no single one dominant: Republican and Trump fallout (23% of framed items), voter blocs and long-term shifts (23%), Democratic mandate and governing agenda (21%), markets and economy (17%), and live results tracking (15%). Only 47 of 160 items (29%) were assigned a framing, and the divide is rated "unreliable" (kappa 0.5), so the picture is loose rather than polarized.

Framing summaries:
- **Live results:** tallies, maps and charts with little interpretation. Reuters, NBC News, BBC, Yahoo and the Financial Times (tracker) are examples.
- **Democratic mandate:** what Democrats will do with power, such as Supreme Court reform (CBS News), tariff reversal (WSJ) and data center pauses. Several Mastodon accounts also debate Democratic leadership.
- **Republican/Trump fallout:** Politico describes Republican panic over 2028; one account cites Trump blaming the Iran war.
- **Markets:** the Financial Times, France 24 and Japan Times' Mastodon account stress falling stocks and AI-sector worries.
- **Voter blocs:** CNN on progressive Democrats and the Washington Post on historical comparisons.

The data gives no political-lean labels for any outlet or account, so none are assigned.

Limits: outlets are judged only from headlines and snippets, and most have one or two items, flagged as still "building." Sample sizes are small.

narratives.common: President Trump announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Coverage ties the change to the Republican losses in the midterm elections and describes Miller as an immigration hardliner.

groups.distinct: Posts are mostly sarcastic or hostile commentary and use labels like "architect of the brutalization of immigrants" and "fascist", with jokes and shitposts mixed in. One post links the move to Trump's media ban that reportedly caught aides off guard while Wiles was out of town. Others mention Duke and a Colbert segment, and some posts are unrelated to the story.

Mostly short, wire-style headlines that frame the move as a response to the midterm losses and the coming "Dem takeover". One item, from Bloomberg Law, covers a separate story about the FBI ousting officials who probed threats to Miller's wife.

outlets: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
outlet_notes: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos: center-left (AI estimate)

groups.distinct: Frames the appointment as Trump "doubling down" on a hard-line agenda after a "midterm rout". Opinion and feature outlets are sharper: Mother Jones says "Hell on Earth" and WIRED asks how Miller "schemed his way to the top". The Atlantic also describes it as doubling down.

Adds local and institutional angles: NBC Los Angeles notes Miller is "of Santa Monica" and the Duke Chronicle claims him as an alumnus. A House.gov item carries a statement from Rep. Jayapal, and Yahoo folds it into live midterm results coverage with Alaska and Mississippi still undecided. ABC7 stresses that Wiles is "out".

There is little direct news coverage. Comments mention Miller in passing, alongside Hegseth and Russ Vought, in broader arguments about Project 2025, immigration enforcement and racism. Other comments are off-topic.

Uses stronger verbs, saying Trump "sacks" Wiles and that she "resigns". The Times of India headline quotes "STEPHEN MILLER IS A DISASTER" and says Trump was "cornered on cam". The Hindu and ThePrint stay closer to the standard framing of a replacement or promotion.
Explainer format: "Who is Stephen Miller?" pieces profile him as an immigration hardliner. Livemint adds his views on Iran, Venezuela and Greenland.

Brief and neutral. The Financial Times uses "immigration hardliner", and the Belfast Telegraph leads with the "new White House chief of staff" and the midterm defeat without naming Miller in its headline.

conflicts: Indian media says Trump "sacks" Wiles (India Today) and that she "resigns" (Times of India), while US outlets describe a replacement or a departure.

narrative:
Coverage of Trump naming Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff divides into four framings, and the divide is rated strong (kappa 0.55). Of 160 items, 59 (37%) carried a framing. Reaction to midterm losses is the largest at 34%. It ties the change to Republican defeats and sometimes uses words like "rout." Neutral personnel announcements follow at 31%. Promotion/profile pieces account for 19%, and alarm about Miller's influence for 17%. The alarm framing quotes a former Trump aide calling the prospect "terrifying."

Outlet labels come only from a few headlines each. BBC, Bloomberg, ABC News, Axios, Politico and The Washington Post lean neutral. NDTV, The Times of India, The Times of Israel, AP and PBS lean toward the midterm framing. Reuters, CBS News and The Guardian lean toward promotion/profile. CNN leans neutral. The Times of India also has one alarm-framed item.

Among Mastodon accounts, several posts use the midterm framing. Others, such as drmike, Nonilex and scheichsbeutel, use the alarm framing.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets, and every outlet and account has 1–2 items, below the thresholds the tool needs for firm labels. Samples are small.
